a. 8 electrons (4 shared pairs – four N–H bonds).
b. A shared (bonding) pair is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms in a covalent bond; a lone (non-bonding) pair is a pair of outer-shell electrons on one atom that is not used in bonding.
c. A dative (coordinate) bond is a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom (e.g. the N lone pair donated to H⁺).

questions.section: PART TWO Structured Questions (10 X 6=60 marks)
questions.question:
6. A compound has the empirical formula CH₂O and relative M mass of 180.
   (RAM= C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)
  a. Define.
     i) Empirical formula. (1 Marks)
     ii) Molecular formula. (1 Marks)
  b. Calculate the empirical formula mass. (2 Marks)
  c. Calculate the molecular formula of the above compound. (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. i) Empirical formula – the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
   ii) Molecular formula – the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
b. CH₂O = 12 + 2(1) + 16 = 30
c. n = 180/30 = 6 → (CH₂O)₆ = C₆H₁₂O₆

questions.section: PART TWO Structured Questions (10 X 6=60 marks)
questions.question:
7. The table below shows the number of protons and electrons of several particles.

   Particles | # protons | # electrons
   A         | 12        | 10
   B         | 17        | 18
   C         | 10        | 10
   D         | 3         | 2

  a. Which of the above particles are positive ions? (2 Marks)
  b. Which of the above particles are negative ions? (2 Marks)
  c. Which of the above particles are neutral atoms? (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. A (Mg²⁺) and D (Li⁺) – more protons than electrons.
b. B (Cl⁻) – more electrons than protons.
c. C (Ne) – equal numbers of protons and electrons.

diagram.caption: Blast furnace: iron ore, coke and limestone enter at the top, hot air is blown in near the bottom, hot waste gases leave at the top, and molten iron and slag are run off through separate tap holes.

questions.answer_guide:
a. Iron ore (haematite, Fe₂O₃), coke (carbon), limestone (calcium carbonate) and hot air.
b. Molten iron and slag (calcium silicate); waste gases also leave the top.
c. Any two: making steel; construction (bridges, buildings, reinforcing bars); making tools, machinery, vehicles and pipes.

questions.section: PART TWO Structured Questions (10 X 6=60 marks)
questions.question:
10. Calcium Carbonate can breakdown into Calcium Oxide and Carbon dioxide:-
   Calcium Carbonate → Calcium Oxide + Calcium dioxide
  a. Write the balanced Chemical equation of the above reaction? (2 Marks)
  b. What are conditions needed for the above reaction to take place? (2 Marks)
  c. State any two uses of Calcium Oxide? (2 Marks)
questions.answer_guide:
a. CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)
b. Strong heating (high temperature, about 800–1000 °C) – thermal decomposition, e.g. in a lime kiln.
c. Any two: making cement and mortar; neutralising acidic soils; making slaked lime (calcium hydroxide); flux in steel making; drying agent.
